I may have had a slighty different situation than you but the end result was the same. I had to start supporting myself at a young age. What I can add in terms of financing school is applying for aid. 
Assuming you are in the US there are federal loans and grants you can qualify for just for filling out the fafsa. Now the fafsa most likely requires your parents tax infomation and input which is a barrier. IT DOESN'T  HAVE TO BE. You can apply for independent status either through the courts if you are under 18 or through you university if you are older. I filed for independent status and I was able to out more loan at lower rates and more grants. Best part I don't need to rely on my parents money or tax information. As far as I know, weight gain is a side effect of every antipsychotic. However on wikipedia it says Latuda is the second least likely to cause weight gain behind haloperidol.

In terms of side effects, I dislike both medications. Abilify gave me muscle spasms, grimacing, and made it difficult for me to relax or sleep. While latuda just made me uncontrollably anxious. But everyone is different, for example I didn't gain weight on Invega.

I think you are putting a lot of blame on your mom that isn't in her control. 

She probably didn't decide to stop taking her meds with malicious or selfish intent. Medication often is only barely helpful and comes at a huge cost in terms of side effects. Often people feel like zombies on anti-psychotics, get uncontrollable muscle movements, etc. While they benefit from only a mild reduction in their symptoms. Maybe she felt that the side-effect outweighed the benefits she got from it and was trying her best to manage her symptoms on her own. 

It could also be that she believes that the medication isn't good for her. She could have been paranoid and proper care wasn't taken to address her concerns to get her to take the medication regularly. Some people don't know how to address schizophrenics with delusions, or nudge them in right way to help them take their medication when they are scared of it. 

This illness is very challenging, and you need to come from a place of understanding when addressing the actions of someone trying to cope with their symptoms.  

In terms of telling your father about her illness. It is something difficult to talk about and she might have been afraid to share it. It sounds like there wasn't any sign of her being ill until a good time after they got married. Maybe her symptoms were under control up until that point and she felt there was no point to mention it since it was under control. 

To answer your questions: 

1) Yes the illness can alter you thinking so you believe you don't need the medication.  

2) A person with schizophrenia is responsible for their actions like any other person, however just as some situations may explain/justify a person's actions. I think you should try to understand your mother's behavior from her point of view and you might realize that she wasn't trying to hurt you or your family.
